title: Imitate God (Jeremiah 9:23)
hook: the Guide ends: know God, then practice kindness, justice and righteousness

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: most harm we do. Maimonides sorted suffering into three kinds and found the harm people bring on themselves the most frequent. Did you take responsibility for one thing? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-two.

The final chapter of a long, difficult book. Maimonides has spent the whole Guide for the Perplexed on hard questions: what words about God can mean, how prophecy works, why the commandments exist. A reader turning to the last pages might expect one last proof, something sealed and abstract. Instead he sorts out what people chase in life, opens the book of Jeremiah, and lands on three plain Hebrew words: kindness, justice, righteousness. A whole philosophy ends at the door of an ordinary deed. This week ends there too, with today's word.
screen: `THE GUIDE'S LAST CHAPTER.` → `ONE LAST PROOF?` → `KINDNESS, JUSTICE, RIGHTEOUSNESS.`

segments.voice: Imitate God. Turn that last chapter four ways. First, four things people call perfection. Maimonides lists them in order: what you own, the health and strength of your body, good character, and finally true knowledge of God. Possessions can be gone overnight, he says, and they were never really part of you. A strong body is something an animal has too. Good character is precious, but it mostly matters in how you deal with other people. Knowledge of God is the one that is truly your own. Second, the prophet seems to agree. He quotes Jeremiah: "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom," nor the mighty in his might, nor the rich in his riches. Glory instead, the prophet says, in understanding and knowing God. So far it sounds as if the mind is the finish line. Third, the verse keeps going. Jeremiah doesn't stop at knowing God. He says what kind of God: the LORD who does mercy, justice and righteousness in the earth, "for in these things I delight, saith the LORD." In Hebrew, chesed, mishpat, tzedakah. Maimonides slows down here. The goal, he says, is to know God's ways, and whoever comes to know them will set out to act the same way. Fourth, this is a commandment, not only an ideal. In his law code he counts it from Deuteronomy, "and walk in His ways," and he gives the rabbis' explanation: as God is called gracious, be gracious; as God is called merciful, be merciful. So the book written for a perplexed student ends with a person getting up to do one kind thing. The knowing is meant to show up in the doing.
screen: `FOUR KINDS OF PERFECTION.` · `NOT WISDOM, MIGHT OR RICHES.` · `MERCY, JUSTICE, RIGHTEOUSNESS.` · `WALK IN HIS WAYS.` · then, large: `FOR IN THESE THINGS I DELIGHT.`

segments.voice: Let the breath slow down, and get comfortable. Bring to mind the people you'll see in the next day. One of them could use something small: a ride, a message, a meal, a fair hearing, an apology you owe. Don't pick the grandest thing. Pick the one you would actually do. See yourself doing it, start to finish. If you pray, you can hold the words "and walk in His ways" for a few breaths. Then let the picture go and simply sit. The bell holds the time.
Imitate God. The Guide's ending: come to know God's ways, then act in them, with kindness, justice and righteousness. Today's word.
Your line: knowledge leads to kindness. Today, do the one kindness you chose. This week ran from silence before God to walking in God's ways. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Jewish teaching often links knowing God with walking in God's ways, and some communities study the Guide's last chapter alongside acts of kindness, justice and charity in daily life.

notes: Title says Jeremiah 9:23 (JPS/Hebrew numbering); the passage is Jeremiah 9:22–23 in JPS 1917 and 9:23–24 in the KJV. Sources use JPS numbering.

Guide 3:54 paraphrased: the four perfections (possessions, body, moral character, intellectual knowledge of God), moral perfection as mainly for dealings with others, and the reading of Jeremiah's chesed, mishpat, tzedakah as the call to imitate God's ways. Please confirm.

JPS 1917 quotations: confirm exact wording and capitalization of 'Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom', 'for in these things I delight, saith the LORD' (JPS prints poetry with line-initial capitals; lowercased here mid-sentence), and 'and walk in His ways'.
Hilchot De'ot 1:5–6: walking in God's ways counted as a commandment, with the rabbinic 'as He is called gracious, be gracious' explanation, paraphrased. Please confirm.
